solution: I am a preschool teacher. During lessons, I noticed that one child always counted differently; while the others counted "1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7," she would say "1, 2, 3, 7," skipping the numbers in between. When I tried to correct her, she insisted that her mother had taught her that way. Uncertain about this, I proposed a home visit. Her mother took me to a hospital instead; it turned out she was suffering from heart disease and had only a few days left to live. It was March, and her daughter’s birthday was in July; she had told this "white lie" so that she could be there to celebrate one last birthday with her child. Deeply moved by this revelation, I decided to play along and told her, just as her mother had, that the number following 3 is indeed 7.
canonical_facts: A preschool teacher hears a child count 1,2,3,7 and learns the mother taught it
On requesting a home visit the teacher is taken to a hospital
The mother is terminally ill with heart disease and has only days left
It is March but the child’s birthday is in July
The mother pretends to skip the intervening months to share one last birthday
The sympathetic teacher then repeats that 7 comes after 3
explicit_negatives: The mother, not the child, is terminally ill. The month skipping is pretend; ordinary numerical order has not changed.
unknown_details: The child’s exact age, hospital name and eventual medical outcome are unspecified. The story is a pretense, not literal time travel.
